nodes.title: Exploitation techniques: Key Ideas
nodes.content: The exploitation phase of a pentest is where reconnaissance becomes access. You're chaining a vulnerability with a payload to land code execution. The exam tests common categories (buffer overflows, injection, deserialization, privilege escalation) and the tools that automate them.

flashcards.front: Buffer overflow — what's the basic mechanism?
flashcards.back: An unbounded write past the end of a stack buffer overwrites the saved return address. When the function returns, execution jumps to whatever the attacker placed there — typically shellcode or a return-into-libc gadget. Modern mitigations: stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX — defeated one at a time by chaining bugs.

flashcards.front: SQL injection vs command injection — same idea?
flashcards.back: Same root cause: untrusted input concatenated into a command string the interpreter executes. SQLi puts `OR 1=1` into a query. Command injection puts `; cat /etc/passwd` into a shell call. Mitigations also the same shape: parameterized queries, never build commands by string concatenation.

flashcards.front: What is privilege escalation?
flashcards.back: Going from a low-priv shell to root / SYSTEM / admin. Two flavors: vertical (low → high on the same machine via a kernel bug, sudo misconfig, SUID binary) and horizontal (account A → account B at same privilege level). The 'pentester's daily bread' — initial access is usually a low-priv user.

flashcards.front: Why is Metasploit so commonly mentioned in exam questions?
flashcards.back: It's the dominant exploit framework — modular: pick an exploit module, set a payload (Meterpreter, reverse shell), set options (RHOSTS, LHOST), run. It bundles thousands of vetted exploits and post-modules. The exam tests vocabulary (msfconsole, payload, listener, handler) more than deep usage.

questions.q: A penetration tester on the same open Wi-Fi network as a target uses ARP spoofing to redirect the target's traffic through the tester's laptop before forwarding it to the hotel gateway, capturing session cookies in transit. Which class of attack does this scenario describe?
choices: Replay attack — re-submitting captured authentication tokens to impersonate the original user after the session ends
Man-in-the-middle attack — covertly inserting between two parties to observe or alter their communications undetected
Denial-of-service attack — flooding gateway resources with spoofed packets to prevent other guests from connecting
Credential stuffing — cycling through a leaked username-password list against the hotel portal's authentication endpoint
questions.explanation: ARP spoofing lets the attacker silently relay traffic between the victim and the gateway while reading or modifying it — the defining characteristic of a man-in-the-middle attack. A replay attack reuses previously captured tokens after a session ends; it does not involve real-time interception and relay of live traffic.

questions.q: A security researcher analyzes a crash dump from a legacy C-based file parsing library. The debugger shows the instruction pointer holds a value sourced directly from the user-supplied test file, and adjacent fields on the stack frame contain bytes from the parsed input. ASLR and stack canaries were both disabled. Which vulnerability class BEST describes the root cause?
choices: Integer overflow — arithmetic wraps past the integer type's maximum value, silently corrupting a calculation and potentially overwriting adjacent values in memory — this is an arithmetic flaw, not a case where input data exceeds a buffer's allocated bounds
Buffer overflow — input data exceeds the allocated buffer's bounds, overwriting adjacent memory and altering control flow
Format string vulnerability — attacker-controlled printf specifiers expose or overwrite adjacent memory locations directly through the format string, not by exceeding an allocated buffer's bounds
Use-after-free — freed heap memory is accessed via a dangling pointer after reallocation, letting attackers influence object contents
questions.explanation: A buffer overflow occurs when a write operation exceeds the bounds of its allocated buffer, overwriting adjacent memory — in this scenario, bytes from the input file overwrote the stack frame and redirected the instruction pointer. Integer overflows are a distinct arithmetic class that can sometimes precede buffer overflows but are a different root cause. Format string vulnerabilities exploit printf-family format specifiers, not buffer bounds. Use-after-free involves accessing freed heap memory, a separate memory-safety class from stack-based buffer overflows.

questions.q: An incident response team traces a breach to a code-signed update for a widely used network-monitoring product pushed through the vendor's normal release channel. Forensics show the malicious build was assembled inside the vendor's CI/CD pipeline weeks earlier, then signed with the vendor's legitimate publisher certificate before being pushed to customers. Which attack class BEST describes this scenario?
choices: Supply chain attack — adversary compromises a trusted supplier and weaponises a normal signed release
Watering-hole attack — adversary poisons a site the victims frequent so a normal release-day visit triggers exploit
Drive-by download — exploit served to any visitor of a poisoned page, unrelated to a vendor's release pipeline
Insider threat — a privileged employee deliberately corrupts the normal release before the build is signed
questions.explanation: Supply chain attacks target trusted software vendors. Attackers compromise a legitimate software update or hardware component, affecting all downstream customers who trust and install it. Very difficult to detect.

questions.q: A red-team report describes lateral movement inside a Windows domain. The attacker captured an NTLM hash from a workstation's LSASS memory and used it directly against an admin share on a different server. At no point was the plaintext password recovered or cracked, but the second host accepted the authentication. Which Windows-credentials attack is being demonstrated?
choices: Pass-the-ticket — replaying a captured Kerberos TGT obtained from a domain controller, no NTLM hash used
Golden ticket — forging a Kerberos TGT directly signed with the captured KRBTGT account NTLM hash
Pass-the-hash — replaying the captured NTLM hash directly to authenticate as the user
Kerberoasting — requesting service tickets and cracking them offline, NTLM hash captured later
questions.explanation: In Windows, NTLM authentication sends the hash, not the password. An attacker who captures a hash can use it directly to authenticate. Mitigations: Credential Guard, LAPS, disable NTLM where possible.

questions.q: A security analyst reviewing authentication logs observes thousands of failed login attempts against a single account over two hours. Each attempt uses a different password following an alphabetical sequence: 'aaaa', 'aaab', 'aaac'. No leaked credential data was involved, and account lockout was disabled by a misconfiguration. Which attack type BEST describes this pattern?
choices: Password spraying — tests one commonly used password across many accounts in sequence from a list, rather than testing every possible character combination against a single account

Credential stuffing — replays known username-password pairs from a publicly leaked breach database against target accounts in sequence — this uses a pre-existing breach list rather than testing every possible character combination in a sequential brute-force sweep
Dictionary attack — iterates through a curated wordlist of likely passwords and phrases rather than exhaustively testing every possible sequential character combination from scratch
Brute force attack — tests every possible character combination in sequence until the correct credential is found, without relying on wordlists or prior breach data
questions.explanation: The alphabetical sequential pattern ('aaaa', 'aaab'...) is the defining characteristic of brute force — it tests every combination without any prior knowledge of which passwords are likely. A dictionary attack would show wordlist entries like 'password123'; credential stuffing would use real email-password pairs from a breach; password spraying would target many accounts with one common password rather than exhausting all combinations against a single account.

questions.q: A SOC analyst sees thousands of overnight login failures against the company login page. Each attempt uses a distinct account/secret pair, many matching real users in the directory. Threat intelligence correlates the pairs to a recent third-party breach. Which attack technique BEST describes what is happening right now?
choices: Credential stuffing — replaying leaked credentials at the portal
Credential harvesting — building the upstream list via phishing or breach dumps
Password spraying — one common password tried slowly against many accounts
Brute force — exhaustively iterating every possible password for one account
questions.explanation: The portal is being hit with a list of pre-existing username/password pairs from a third-party breach — that is the textbook definition of credential stuffing. Credential harvesting is the upstream collection step (phishing, dumps, keyloggers) that produced the list, not the activity at the portal. Password spraying uses one common password across many accounts (rotation pattern is different). Brute force iterates passwords against a single account.

questions.q: An online-banking user reports that funds transfers appear to leave the account for a different recipient than what was entered in the browser form. Forensic capture of the user's session shows the HTTPS connection to the bank is intact, but the transaction payload is being altered AFTER the user clicks Send and BEFORE it leaves the browser. Which threat BEST fits the evidence?
choices: Man-in-the-browser malware — code inside the browser tampers with form data inside the user's session
Hardware keylogger — a physical device captures keystrokes from the user's input session
Stored XSS in a browser extension — injects script into the page during the browsing session
SQL injection in the banking backend — a crafted form value alters the query for that user's session
questions.explanation: MITB attacks (e.g., ZeuS, SpyEye) infect the browser via malicious extensions or process injection. They intercept banking transactions after the user authenticates, modifying payee/amount before submission.

questions.q: A red-team report describes the operators' tradecraft: encoding payloads in base64, hiding command-and-control inside DNS queries, modifying file timestamps to match neighbouring system files, clearing event logs, and relying on built-in Windows utilities (PowerShell, WMI) instead of dropping new executables. Which umbrella category captures these techniques?
choices: Physical pretexting used to gain initial access to a facility
Defence-evasion and anti-forensics, including living-off-the-land binaries
Network compression to reduce bandwidth used by exfiltrated payloads
Distributed denial-of-service mitigation deployed at the network edge
questions.explanation: All techniques listed (encoding, DNS C2, timestomping, log clearing, LotL) are post-compromise tactics to evade detection and frustrate forensics. ATT&CK groups them under the Defense Evasion tactic. Pretexting is a social-engineering initial-access technique. The remaining options are unrelated to attacker tradecraft.

correct.useCase: Aggregate and correlate logs from across the environment for real-time alerting and investigation.

distractors.useCase: Enroll and patch endpoints and enforce device compliance.
Verify firmware and boot integrity at startup.
Block network intrusions inline at the firewall.

nodes.title: Cryptography fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Crypto is the math layer that makes the rest of security possible. Most exam questions test symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, when to use which, and how key management actually works in practice.

flashcards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Symmetric (AES-256, ChaCha20): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private key pair, slow, used to exchange a symmetric key or to sign. Real systems use both: asymmetric to negotiate, symmetric to encrypt the bulk traffic (this is how TLS works).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
flashcards.back: Encryption is reversible — the holder of the key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is one-way — you cannot derive the input from the output. Hashes are for integrity (did the file change?) and password storage (compare hashes, never store plaintext). SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

flashcards.front: What is a digital signature?
flashcards.back: A signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the signer's private key. Anyone with the public key can verify (decrypt the signature, recompute the hash, check they match). This proves authenticity (the holder of the private key signed it) AND integrity (the message wasn't tampered with).

flashcards.front: Why use a key management service (KMS)?
flashcards.back: Raw key handling is hard to do safely — you have to rotate, audit, restrict, destroy. A KMS holds keys in hardware, exposes encrypt/decrypt APIs, logs every use, enforces who can use which key. Your application code never sees the actual key material. AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS all play this role.

questions.q: A cloud security architect is designing a system where remote contractors must authenticate to internal APIs. The solution must issue short-lived credentials signed by an internal trust anchor, support immediate revocation when a contractor is terminated, and let relying parties verify credential authenticity offline without querying the issuer on each request. Which framework encompasses the trust anchor, registration process, and revocation mechanisms in this design?
choices: LDAP — a directory service protocol that stores and retrieves identity attributes but provides no certificate-issuance framework and has no built-in certificate revocation mechanism
Kerberos — a ticket-based authentication system in which a Key Distribution Center grants short-lived service tickets on a per-session basis
PKI — a framework of certificate authorities and revocation infrastructure governing the full digital-certificate lifecycle
RADIUS — a centralized AAA protocol that authenticates users and authorizes network access against credentials held in a shared back-end store
questions.explanation: PKI provides the complete infrastructure — including certificate authority (CA) hierarchy, registration authority (RA), certificate revocation lists (CRL), and OCSP — for issuing, distributing, and revoking X.509 digital certificates. Kerberos provides mutual authentication using tickets rather than certificates and does not provide a certificate revocation mechanism, making it unsuitable when credentials must be verifiably invalidated before expiry.

questions.q: A financial application encrypts gigabytes of transaction logs at rest and uses TLS to protect connections between its app server and clients over the public internet. During a code review a developer asks why two different encryption methods are required. Which statement correctly explains the design choice?
choices: Symmetric algorithms (e.g., AES) encrypt bulk data efficiently with a shared key; asymmetric algorithms (e.g., RSA/ECDH) negotiate that shared key across the untrusted channel
Asymmetric algorithms handle bulk data with lower CPU overhead than symmetric; symmetric encryption is reserved for verifying digital signatures during the TLS handshake only
Both algorithm types require a pre-shared key established out-of-band; the distinction is driven entirely by key length, not by performance or operational use-case differences
Symmetric encryption cannot protect data at rest and is limited to in-transit traffic, so asymmetric algorithms handle storage while symmetric is used solely for the TLS handshake
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) uses the same key for both encryption and decryption, making it highly efficient for large data volumes such as transaction logs stored at rest. Asymmetric encryption (e.g., RSA, ECDH) uses a key pair so that two parties can securely agree on a shared session key without ever transmitting it — this is why TLS uses asymmetric for the handshake and symmetric for bulk data transfer. Option B is incorrect because asymmetric algorithms are orders of magnitude slower than symmetric and are never used for bulk data encryption.

questions.q: A PKI engineer is tasked with updating the organization's internal certificate authority to align with current NIST cryptographic transition requirements. The existing CA signs certificate requests using SHA-1. Which algorithm should replace SHA-1 for all new signing operations?
choices: MD5 — 128-bit output, widely supported and computationally efficient for bulk certificate issuance

SHA-1 — 160-bit output, still accepted by some legacy CAs for internal non-public certificates, but deprecated for new digital signing operations and no longer considered a current NIST-approved algorithm for PKI signing
SHA-256 — current NIST standard for new digital signatures; approved for all PKI signing operations
BLAKE2b — faster than SHA-256 with equivalent output size, but absent from the NIST approved list for PKI use
questions.explanation: NIST deprecated SHA-1 for digital signature generation and mandates SHA-256 or stronger (SHA-2/SHA-3 family) for new certificate signing operations. MD5 was deprecated even earlier due to demonstrated collision vulnerabilities. BLAKE2b is cryptographically strong but is not included in NIST SP 800-131A's approved algorithm list for PKI signing, making it unsuitable for a compliance-aligned CA.

questions.q: A forensics team obtains a multi-year archive of a company's TLS-encrypted traffic and legally acquires the web server's long-term private key. They discover the archived sessions still cannot be decrypted. Which TLS feature explains this outcome?
choices: Certificate pinning — the client hardcodes the expected server certificate fingerprint to prevent MITM substitution — pinning validates the certificate identity but does not prevent past session records from being decrypted if the long-term private key is later compromised
Perfect forward secrecy — ephemeral session keys are discarded after use; past recordings cannot be decrypted
HSTS preloading — the browser enforced HTTPS connections but this policy does not protect past recorded sessions
OCSP stapling — the CA validates certificate revocation status in real time but does not affect session key recoverability
questions.explanation: Perfect forward secrecy (PFS) uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDHE) to derive a unique session key that is discarded immediately after the session ends — even possessing the server's long-term private key cannot reconstruct it, so archived ciphertext is permanently unreadable. Certificate pinning, HSTS, and OCSP stapling are valuable TLS controls but none of them affect whether historical session keys can be recovered after the fact.

questions.q: A SOC analyst examining exfiltrated data finds a JPEG of an office party uploaded to a public-facing photo-sharing site. A forensic extraction shows the file contains an embedded ZIP archive of customer records hidden in the image's least-significant bits, undetectable to the human eye. The file passes content-inspection filters because its visible payload is a normal photo. Which exfiltration technique is in use?
choices: DNS tunneling — encoding the image's data into DNS queries to a controlled name server to evade content inspection — DNS tunneling encodes arbitrary data in DNS but does not embed the data inside a carrier image file
Asymmetric encryption with a public key — the file is encrypted but its presence is not hidden, image content visible
ICMP covert channel — embedding the file's bytes in ping payloads, no image carrier needed
Steganography — hiding the data inside an innocuous image carrier file to defeat content inspection
questions.explanation: Steganography hides messages within cover files. Example: embedding secret text in the least significant bits of image pixels. Different from encryption — encryption hides the content; steganography hides the existence.

questions.q: A penetration tester is auditing a system that uses a 64-bit hash for user-session tokens. The tester wants to find two different session payloads that produce the same hash, allowing one to be substituted for another. Statistical analysis shows roughly 2^32 attempts are needed before a collision is overwhelmingly likely. Which cryptographic attack class does this exploit?
choices: Pre-image attack — find any input that produces a specific target hash, brute over the full hash space
Second pre-image attack — given an input, find a different input with the same hash (full hash space)
Birthday attack
Side-channel attack — measure hash-operation timing on the target device to leak internal state bits
questions.explanation: The birthday paradox: the probability of two people sharing a birthday reaches 50% at just 23 people. Similarly, hash collisions are found much faster than expected. MD5 is broken; SHA-256 provides much higher collision resistance.

questions.q: A software publisher wants every customer's installer to carry a verifiable claim binding (1) the publisher's identity and (2) the integrity of the binary as released — so that any modification by an attacker after release is detected by the operating system at install time. Which control is being described?
choices: TLS server certificates issued to the download CDN's hostname
A code-signing certificate issued to the vendor and applied to the installer
S/MIME certificates issued to the developers who built the release
A SHA-256 hash posted on the download page next to the installer link
questions.explanation: Code-signing certificates bind the publisher's identity to the binary via a digital signature, which the OS verifies before installation. Any post-release modification breaks the signature. TLS certs authenticate the download host, not the artefact itself. S/MIME signs email, not executables. A posted hash gives integrity but no bound publisher identity — anyone could post a different hash for a different binary.

questions.q: A payments processor must meet PCI-DSS key-management requirements: the master encryption key for cardholder data must (1) be generated inside tamper-resistant hardware, (2) NEVER leave that hardware in plaintext, and (3) sign/encrypt operations are performed by sending data INTO the device. Which device category satisfies all three requirements?
choices: USB encrypted thumb-drive hardware — a tamper-resistant device for files, not for non-exportable keys
Hardware Security Module (HSM) — a tamper-resistant device that generates and uses keys in-place
Software cryptographic library — runs on commodity hardware, not a tamper-resistant key device
Network firewall hardware — a perimeter device, tamper-resistant chassis but not a key-custody device
questions.explanation: An HSM is a tamper-resistant, FIPS-140-validated device whose private keys are non-exportable; applications send data IN and get signed/encrypted output back. USB drives store data, not non-exportable keys. Software libraries hold keys in process memory. A firewall is perimeter security, unrelated to key custody. NOTE: prior version of this question had the wrong correct-answer index (described a firewall appliance as the HSM definition) — fixed during the 2026-05-13 audit pass.

nodes.title: Order the incident response lifecycle

data.scenario: Put the incident response phases in order, from before an incident occurs through closing it out.

nodes.explanation: The incident response process runs Preparation -> Identification -> Containment -> Eradication -> Recovery -> Lessons Learned. Containment always comes before eradication, and lessons learned closes the loop so you improve before the next incident.

nodes.title: VPN and secure connectivity: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPN tunnels private traffic over the public internet, encrypting it end-to-end. Site-to-site VPNs connect networks (e.g., on-prem to cloud); client VPNs connect individual devices to a private network. Both rely on IPsec or SSL/TLS.

flashcards.front: Site-to-site VPN vs client VPN — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Site-to-site VPN connects two networks (typical: on-prem data center ↔ cloud VPC) using gateway devices on each side. Client VPN connects an individual user's laptop to a private network for remote access. Site-to-site uses IPsec, client VPN often uses SSL or WireGuard.

flashcards.front: IPsec — IKE phase 1 vs phase 2.
flashcards.back: Phase 1 (IKE) authenticates the two peers (pre-shared key or certificate) and builds a secure management channel. Phase 2 negotiates the actual data tunnel (encryption algorithm, key lifetime). Most exam questions test that phase 1 must succeed before phase 2.

flashcards.front: When do you pick a dedicated link over a VPN?
flashcards.back: VPN over the public internet is cheap but variable — bandwidth and latency depend on internet weather. Dedicated links (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Cloud Interconnect) are private fiber with consistent latency and bandwidth — pick them for production traffic that must be predictable, or compliance scenarios that forbid the public internet.

flashcards.front: What's the BGP tunnel option for?
flashcards.back: VPNs can use static routes or BGP. BGP-based VPNs auto-propagate route changes between sides (add a new subnet on-prem → cloud learns it within seconds). Static VPN requires manual route updates every time the topology changes. Always pick BGP for production.

questions.q: A network engineer deploys a security appliance in span/mirror-port mode off a core switch so it receives a copy of all traffic passing through. The appliance evaluates packets against known attack signatures and sends real-time alerts to the SOC dashboard. When the SOC reviews a flagged brute-force login attempt, they discover the attack traffic reached the authentication server unimpeded. Why did the appliance not stop the attack?
choices: The appliance is a next-generation firewall (NGFW) that requires updated threat-intelligence feeds — an NGFW inspects and blocks packets inline; it does not operate out-of-band and generates policy-enforcement actions rather than passive alerts on suspicious packets
The appliance is an IDS, which operates out-of-band on mirrored traffic and generates alerts but cannot intercept or drop live packets
The appliance is a web application firewall (WAF), which only inspects HTTP/HTTPS application-layer payloads and ignores non-web authentication traffic
The appliance is a security information and event management (SIEM) system, which aggregates and correlates log data but does not sit in the traffic path
questions.explanation: An IDS operates in passive/out-of-band mode: it receives a copy of traffic via a span or tap, analyzes it, and raises alerts, but it has no ability to drop or modify packets flowing on the live network. An IPS, by contrast, is placed inline in the traffic path so it can intercept and block malicious packets in real time — the key functional difference the scenario is testing.

questions.q: Remote engineers connect to corporate resources over public Wi-Fi. The security team needs every byte between laptop and HQ encrypted, with mutual peer authentication and a routed path into internal subnets. Which technology meets this need?
choices: A TLS-only forward web proxy serving HTTPS browsing traffic
A stateful perimeter firewall enforcing inbound access-control rules
An IPSec or SSL-based VPN client with certificate-based endpoint auth
An SD-WAN appliance applying QoS marking across inter-branch traffic
questions.explanation: A VPN client establishes an authenticated, encrypted tunnel between the remote laptop and HQ and routes traffic into internal subnets — exactly the three requirements. IPSec (IKEv2) and SSL/TLS (OpenVPN, WireGuard) are the standard protocols. A web proxy only relays HTTP/S and does not route arbitrary subnets. A firewall enforces policy but is not itself the encrypted tunnel. SD-WAN solves site-to-site bandwidth and QoS — not remote-user encryption.

questions.q: A retail company's POS terminals, corporate workstations, and internal file servers all share a flat Layer 2 network with no VLAN separation. After a POS malware incident, forensics shows the attacker pivoted directly from the infected terminal to the HR file server. Which architectural change would have MOST limited the attacker's ability to move laterally after the initial POS compromise?
choices: Deploy a next-generation firewall at the internet edge to inspect and block inbound threats — a perimeter firewall does not segment internal VLAN boundaries or isolate POS terminals from HR workstations sharing the same corporate flat network
Implement VLAN segmentation with inter-zone ACLs to isolate POS terminals from HR servers and corporate workstations on separate broadcast domains
Enable endpoint detection and response on all POS terminals to detect malware and automatically isolate infected hosts before lateral movement to adjacent systems can occur

Require 802.1X certificate-based port authentication on all switch ports in every VLAN — 802.1X validates network identity at the port level but does not create VLAN segmentation boundaries or apply inter-zone ACLs on the corporate network to isolate POS traffic
questions.explanation: Network segmentation with VLANs and inter-zone firewall rules contains lateral movement — a POS terminal in its own isolated zone cannot reach HR servers unless a rule explicitly permits that path. A perimeter firewall (option A) would not have helped here because both the initial compromise and the subsequent pivot occurred entirely on the internal network, after the attacker was already inside the perimeter.

questions.q: A NOC is buying a new perimeter security appliance. Vendor A's device sits inline and DROPS packets that match malicious signatures. Vendor B's device sits on a SPAN port, ALERTS on the same signatures but cannot stop the traffic. Which AI/IPS distinction does this describe and which vendor is which?
choices: Both vendors offer IPS — both inspect inline; difference is throughput class only
Both vendors offer IDS — both passive; difference is signature update cadence
Vendor A = IPS (inline, blocks); Vendor B = IDS (passive, alerts only)
Vendor A = IDS (alerts on the SPAN port); Vendor B = IPS (drops inline)
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts — doesn't block. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and blocks malicious traffic in real time. Both use signatures and anomaly detection.

questions.q: An e-commerce site behind an internet load balancer is hit weekly with SQL-injection, cross-site-scripting, and command-injection probes against its HTTP and HTTPS endpoints. The security team wants a Layer-7 control that inspects the actual HTTP request body and headers and blocks these application-layer payloads before they reach the EC2 backend — with no application code change. Which control is the right fit?
choices: Next-generation firewall at the perimeter — inspects L3/L4 traffic but does not block command-injection HTTP payloads
Endpoint protection on the application servers — catches malware after the command-injection request reaches them
Bandwidth-shaping QoS appliance — shapes the application traffic but blocks no SQLi / XSS / command-injection
Web Application Firewall — inspects HTTP/S and blocks SQLi / XSS / CSRF / command-injection payloads at L7
questions.explanation: WAF operates at Layer 7 analyzing HTTP request content. Can be deployed as hardware, software, or cloud service (AWS WAF, Cloudflare, ModSecurity). Uses signature and behavioral rules to block web attacks.

questions.q: A national registrar wants resolvers to cryptographically verify that a DNS reply actually came from the authoritative zone and was not forged in transit. The mechanism must publish public keys in the parent zone and sign each record set; encrypting the query itself is out of scope. Which standard meets this need?
choices: DNS firewalling that blocks lookups against reputation lists — a DNS firewall rejects queries to known-malicious domains but does not cryptographically sign responses with public-key infrastructure to prevent spoofing
DNS-over-HTTPS, which encrypts queries between client and resolver
DNSSEC, which signs responses with public-key cryptography
GeoDNS load balancing that returns the closest regional answer
questions.explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS responses with public-key cryptography and chains the keys up through parent zones so resolvers can verify origin and integrity — exactly the requirement. DoH and DoT encrypt the query in flight (privacy) but do not authenticate the underlying record data. DNS firewalls block reputation lists; GeoDNS makes routing decisions. Neither provides origin authentication.

questions.q: A flat-network breach allowed ransomware to spread across an entire /16. The remediation plan splits the network into zones by function (web, app, db, mgmt) at the firewall, AND further isolates each individual workload from its peers using host-level policy (distributed firewalls or SDN labels). The goals are to limit blast radius and prevent worm-style propagation. Which combination is described?
choices: Link aggregation paired with redundant default gateways at the core — improves bandwidth and gateway availability but provides no workload-level isolation or east-west traffic policy enforcement between compute segments
Network function virtualization across consolidated x86 appliances
Network segmentation combined with workload-level microsegmentation
Re-flattening into a single broadcast domain to simplify policy
questions.explanation: Segmentation creates coarse zones at the firewall (VLAN/subnet boundaries). Microsegmentation adds fine-grained per-workload policy (VMware NSX, Cisco ACI, host firewalls) so even peers in the same zone cannot freely talk. The pair is the standard mitigation for worm/lateral-movement risk on a flat network. Link aggregation and NFV target throughput and consolidation, not isolation. Re-flattening is the opposite of the design.

nodes.title: Identity providers and federation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.

questions.q: An IAM design review covers three responsibilities for the new VPN concentrator: (1) verifying who the user is when they connect, (2) deciding what resources that user is allowed to reach, and (3) recording the timestamps and bytes-per-session for compliance audits. The vendor brochure refers to all three as 'AAA'. Which expansion of AAA matches these three responsibilities in order?
choices: Antivirus, Authentication, Authorization — three security A-words but not the AAA spec
Access, Audit, Administration — three IAM-related A-words, also not the AAA spec
Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — the AAA acronym used by RADIUS / TACACS+
Application, API, Authentication — three protocol-layer A-words, not the AAA spec
questions.explanation: AAA: Authentication (verify identity), Authorization (determine what access is permitted), Accounting (log what the user did). RADIUS and TACACS+ are common AAA protocols.

questions.q: A new auth/authz design splits responsibilities between two services. Service A receives the user's credentials, validates the username/password against the IdP, and issues a signed token containing the user's identity claims. Service B reads that token, looks up the user's role + tenant, and decides whether THIS specific request to /api/payouts is allowed. Which split is being described?
choices: Both services do the same job, only the deployment topology differs
Service A authorises before Service B authenticates (zero-trust ordering)
Service A authenticates (confirms the caller's identity)
Both services jointly issue a token that proves identity + grants permissions atomically
questions.explanation: AuthN (authentication) = proving identity (password, fingerprint, certificate). AuthZ (authorization) = what actions/resources are permitted after authentication. Both are required for access control.

questions.q: An admin's MFA enrolment options include: (a) a small physical device (RSA SecurID / YubiKey) that displays or generates a one-time passcode, (b) a smartcard requiring a reader, (c) a TOTP app on the phone, (d) a printed list of recovery codes. The CISO asks specifically for the FIRST option — a dedicated cryptographic device — to be the primary factor for privileged users. What is that device called?
choices: Software password manager — auto-fills credentials, not an MFA device
Hardware security token — standalone OTP device or FIDO2 key separate from the workstation
RFID proximity badge — physical access only, not a remote-auth OTP device
Smartcard — requires a card reader at the workstation, different form factor from a token
questions.explanation: A hardware security token is a physical device (RSA SecurID, YubiKey, hardware OTP) that generates one-time codes or signed assertions for MFA. Distinct from password managers (software, not an auth factor by itself), RFID badges (physical access only), and smartcards (a different form factor with a reader). NOTE: prior version had wrong correct-answer index (marked a mobile password manager as the hardware-token definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.q: A standards body defines a security domain that covers four operations on a subject: (1) identification, (2) authentication, (3) authorisation of subject→object operations, and (4) accounting of those operations. Vendors implement the domain with badge readers, MFA prompts, role bindings, and audit logs. Which domain is being described?
choices: Physical security, since badge readers and surveillance are the obvious case
Access control, covering the identify-authenticate-authorise-account lifecycle
Network firewalling, which decides which packets cross a boundary
Password policy, since credentials are the most common authentication factor
questions.explanation: Access control is the security domain spanning identification, authentication, authorisation, and accounting — often summarised as IAAA or AAA. Badge readers, MFA, RBAC, and audit logs are tactics that implement parts of this domain. Physical security and password policy are subsets/tactics. Firewalling controls packets, not subject↔object authorisation.

questions.q: A SaaS startup wants users to grant a third-party app limited, scoped access to their account (e.g., 'read my calendar, do not send email') without ever sharing their password with the third-party app. The mechanism must support short-lived access tokens, refresh tokens, and scope strings. Which standard fits?
choices: PBKDF2, a key-derivation function used to slow password cracking by iterating a hash — PBKDF2 outputs a derived key, not bearer tokens used in an authorisation-delegation flow
OAuth 2.0, an authorisation-delegation protocol with bearer tokens
SAML 2.0, an SSO assertion exchange between identity and service providers
Mutual TLS, in which client and server present X.509 certificates to each other
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 lets a resource owner authorise a third-party client to receive a scoped, short-lived access token (plus an optional refresh token) — the client never sees the user's password. PBKDF2 is a hash function, not a protocol. SAML is for federated SSO between IdP and SP, not third-party delegation. mTLS authenticates services to each other, with no end-user delegation step.

nodes.title: Vulnerability management (CompTIA CySA+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Vulnerability management is the systematic process of finding, classifying, prioritizing, and remediating security weaknesses before attackers exploit them. CySA+ tests CVSS scoring mechanics, how to prioritize a remediation backlog using risk matrices, the difference between remediation and mitigation, and how credentialed scans differ from unauthenticated ones.

flashcards.front: CVSS Base Score — what metrics feed it?
flashcards.back: Exploitability metrics: Attack Vector (Network/Adjacent/Local/Physical), Attack Complexity (Low/High), Privileges Required (None/Low/High), User Interaction (None/Required). Impact metrics: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability Impact (each None/Low/High). Scope (unchanged/changed) determines if the blast radius crosses a trust boundary. The base score combines these into a 0–10 value; temporal and environmental metrics adjust it for your context.

flashcards.front: Risk prioritization matrix — how do you sequence remediation?
flashcards.back: Plot vulnerabilities on a 2-D matrix: severity (CVSS score) on one axis, exposure/exploitability on the other. Critical + internet-exposed + known exploit (CISA KEV list) = patch immediately. High CVSS but internal-only, no public exploit = patch in the next cycle. Low severity + no network path = defer or accept. Never treat CVSS as a ranking by itself — a 9.8 score behind 3 firewalls may be lower risk than a 7.0 facing the internet.

flashcards.front: Remediation vs mitigation vs acceptance — define each.
flashcards.back: Remediation: permanently fix the vulnerability — apply the patch, rewrite the code, replace the component. Mitigation: reduce exploitability without eliminating the vulnerability — firewall rule, IPS signature, disable the vulnerable feature. Acceptance: formal risk acceptance documented and signed by the data owner when cost of fixing exceeds business impact. Compensating control is a variant of mitigation that satisfies a compliance requirement when the primary control is not feasible.

flashcards.front: Credentialed vs uncredentialed scan — what does each find?
flashcards.back: Uncredentialed (unauthenticated) scan: the scanner probes the network as an outsider — finds open ports, banner-grabbing vulnerabilities, default credentials, and externally exploitable issues. Credentialed scan: the scanner logs in (local admin / SSH key) and reads installed package versions, registry keys, patch levels, and configuration files — finds far more vulnerabilities with very few false positives. Always use credentialed scans on internal systems; uncredentialed scans model attacker perspective from outside.

questions.q: A user receives an email appearing to be from their bank, urging them to click a link and verify their account details. The link leads to a convincing replica of the bank's website hosted on an unfamiliar domain. What type of attack is this?
choices: Vishing — a voice-based attack in which a caller impersonates a trusted institution to extract sensitive information
Pretexting — fabricating a detailed backstory to build trust and manipulate a target into revealing confidential data
Smishing — a text-message lure that directs the recipient to a malicious link or prompts a call-back, unlike email phishing which spoofs a sender address to harvest credentials
Phishing — an email-based attack using a spoofed sender and a counterfeit site to harvest user credentials
questions.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive emails with spoofed senders and lookalike websites to trick users into entering credentials on attacker-controlled pages. Vishing and smishing are closely related social-engineering variants but use voice calls and SMS as the delivery channel, not email.

questions.q: A hospital's file servers become inaccessible over a holiday weekend. Administrators discover every patient-record folder has been encrypted, and a ransom note demands 10 Bitcoin in exchange for the decryption key. Security logs show the encryption was performed by a remote process that spread through a compromised service account. What category of malware caused this incident?
choices: Worm, which self-replicates across network shares by exploiting service vulnerabilities — a worm propagates autonomously but does not encrypt files or demand a ransom payment in exchange for a decryption key
Spyware, which covertly captures user activity and transmits harvested credentials to a remote collection server
Ransomware, which encrypts victim files and withholds the decryption key pending payment of a demanded ransom
Rootkit, which embeds itself in the OS kernel to maintain persistent privileged access while hiding its presence
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and withholds the key until a ransom is paid — the Bitcoin demand and encrypted patient records are defining indicators. A worm also propagates through a network autonomously, but its goal is self-replication and spread, not file encryption for extortion.

questions.q: Threat intelligence analysts discover that attackers are actively exploiting a remote-code-execution flaw in a widely deployed enterprise VPN appliance. The vendor has not yet acknowledged the vulnerability, no CVE identifier has been assigned, and no mitigation guidance is available. How should this vulnerability be classified?
choices: Critical CVE — a flaw formally registered in the NVD with a CVSS score calculated and published by NIST
End-of-life vulnerability — a flaw that persists because the affected version no longer receives vendor patches
Zero-day vulnerability — under active exploitation before the vendor has issued any patch or public acknowledgement
N-day vulnerability — a disclosed flaw for which a vendor patch exists but has not been widely deployed
questions.explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is exploited in the wild before the vendor knows about it and before any patch or official mitigation is available — the absence of a CVE, no vendor acknowledgment, and active exploitation are the key indicators. An n-day differs because the vendor has already disclosed the vulnerability and a patch exists, even if many deployments remain unpatched.

questions.q: An e-commerce platform processing holiday orders observes a sudden flood of HTTP requests originating from thousands of geographically diverse IP addresses. Within minutes, web servers reach 100% CPU utilization, checkout transactions time out, and the load balancer begins dropping connections. The operations team confirms the traffic is composed of synchronized request bursts from ranges associated with known compromised consumer IoT devices. Which attack type best describes this event?
choices: SQL injection — an attacker crafting malicious database queries through unsanitized input fields — this targets database processing but does not involve a traffic flood from compromised external hosts overwhelming the victim's network capacity
Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) — a coordinated traffic flood from many compromised hosts designed to exhaust a target’s processing resources
Credential stuffing — automated submission of breached username-password pairs against authentication endpoints to compromise individual accounts
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) — tricking authenticated users into unknowingly submitting unauthorized requests through their active browser sessions
questions.explanation: A DDoS attack uses a large number of geographically distributed hosts (often a botnet of compromised devices) to flood a target with traffic or requests, overwhelming its resources and denying service to legitimate users — exactly what the synchronized IoT botnet traffic describes. Credential stuffing also leverages distributed sources, but its goal is account takeover through login attempts, not resource exhaustion.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
